articleTitle: Charging of insulator surfaces by ionization and transport in gases
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Insulator surfaces in gases collect charge when the rate of charge arrival exceeds the rate of conduction by the insulator from the surface region. The source of the collected charges may be in close proximity to the surface, and hence greatly influenced by the surface. Alternately, the source may be remote so that it supplies charges independent of the surface accumulation. For the latter arrangement, charge transport processes in the gas greatly influence the charge collected.

articleTitle: Partial discharge evaluation of polyethylene cable material by phase angle and pulse shape anlysis
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: This paper reports on the correlation of chemical and physical deterioration as a result of discharge activity and the partial discharge measurements using only real quantities. Materials investigated are LDPE and peroxide cross-linked polyethylene.

articleTitle: Chemical and discharge effects in plasma etching with freons and other electronegative gases
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Low pressure plasmas of halogens, halo carbons and their mixtures are in general use for etching micron size features on Si, GaAs and InP. Several processing parameters may be varied to attain the optimum conditions for a particular process in terms of etching rates and profile control. The effects of the manipulation of process variables such as pressure, applied frequency, and gas feed composition, are discussed. Specific examples are presented to show these effects in relation to the etching of Si and III–V compounds.

articleTitle: Fundamental and practical limitations on the measurement of corona and partial discharges
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The fundamental limitations on the detection of corona and partial discharges is examined on the basis of relevant communication theory for system noise and pulse detection in noise. The conclusions of this analysis are applied to the detection of corona and partial discharges in lumped-element and simple distributed systems. Optimum system characteristics are described for a number of common detection configurations.

articleTitle: Corona-generated space charge environments in the vicinity of HVDC transmission lines
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Corona discharges occurring on HVDC transmission lines generate ion space charges which fill the entire interelectrode space between the high voltage conductors and the ground plane. In the case of monopolar lines, the polarity of the space charge will be the same as that of the conductor, while in the case of bipolar lines, space charges of both polarities mix in the region between the two conductors.

articleTitle: Electrode degradation in negative point-to-plane corona
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: A model considers the various phenomena occurring in corona at the point electrode and deduces a number of material parameters that would minimize the degradation of this electrode. These parameters are formulated into a figure of merit and point to a number of metals and alloys that should lead to this requirement. Some of these materials are tested and the results are compared with this model.

articleTitle: Particle charging in corona fields
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: This paper contains: 1. A review of the currently accepted theory of particle charging in corona fields in air, by both ionic bombardment and diffusion, in the dark space surrounding the corona glow. 2. Some of the recent findings on particle charging within the corona glow; the study was made possible by the discovery that additives of CO<inf>2</inf> to air in a 5 to 20% range will increase a cylindrical corona glow to a size which is sufficiently large to allow particles to be dropped on various trajectories parallel to the corona wire, and their charge measured. 3. Some of the recent findings on the influence of the shape of the particles when exposed to corona charging.

articleTitle: Silicone elastomer protective coatings for high voltage insulators
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Silicone elastomers are well known for their excellent long term weatherability. This property makes them potentially ideal materials for coating high voltage power transmission insulators exposed to the environment. The concept of coating high voltage insulators with silicones was demonstrated by Niemi at Dow Corning Corporation a few years ago(1). His evaluation utilized various silicone polymer compositions containing different organic substituents on silicon; such as hydrogen, methyl and phenyl. The best silicone composition was found to be an elastomer based on hydrogen and methyl substituted silicone polymers.

articleTitle: EHD instabilities in the breakdown of point-plane gaps in insulating liquids
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Our understanding of the breakdown process in insulating liquids has been advanced considerably by the use of pulsed Schlieren optical techniques to photograph the pre-breakdown events. Experimental work of this type began more than 25 years ago, and Farazmand was the first to publish Schlieren photographs which optically resolved pre-breakdown events of the type shown in Fig. 1.(1) This work was continued by Chadband and co-workers (2,3) who also used a high speed streak camera to check that the pre-breakdown events proceed in an orderly, not a discontinuous manner (without this evidence the work is open to the criticism that single photographs taken from a succession of events do not correctly represent the evolution of a single event).

articleTitle: Influence of electric field and pressure on conduction of polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: We have shown that the compensation law observed in PE between ∼0 and 80°C is due to the linear relation between the activation enthalpy and entropy. Both variables are proportionnal to the volume of activation(as long as it remains small) and which is varying under the influence of pressure and field. ΔH and ΔS are also related to the thermal expansion and compressibility coefficients and to a constant itself related to the Grüneisen constant. The ionic field due to water has been estimated to be ∼1.85 × 10<sup>7</sup> Vm<sup>−1</sup> and it can dominate electrical measurements at low fields. This demonstrates that it is impossible to obtain reproducible or comparable results if the experimental conditions are not completely identical and the desirability of doing measurements under a very good vacuum. One definitive conclusion is that the decrease of ΔH and ΔS under large applied stresses modify considerably the intrinsic properties of the polymer.

articleTitle: Leakage current characteristics of XLPE
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Because the leakage current in XLPE changes in proportion to the quantity of the crosslinking agent by-products, leakage current might be controlled by the amount of ion conduction carriers which are supplied with the by-products. And because the leakage current in impregnated PE sheets changes in proportion to the conductivity of each by-product in liquid, the leakage current in XLPE might also be controlled by the conductivity of each by-product contained in XLPE. The mobility of ion conduction carriers is greatly changed by temperature, but is changed only slightly by stress. This change becomes especially remarkable below the solidification temperature of the crosslinking agent by-products. This might be caused by the change of by-products from the liquid to solid state in XLPE.

articleTitle: Vapor-mist dielectrics
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Although it is well known that particles reduce the strength of many dielectrics, it was recently discovered that a dense mist of micron-size liquid droplets in an insulating gas actually can considerably increase its electrical breakdown strength. As an example, the strength of SF<inf>6</inf> at one atmosphere (0.1 MPa) pressure doubled when mixed with a dense mist of C<inf>2</inf>Cl<inf>4</inf>; and at ∼0.01 MPa pressure, the mist increased the dielectric strength by an order of magnitude. It is believed that the mechanism which these mixtures achieve a high dielectric strength involves supersaturated vapor from the small droplets, the strength of the gas-vapor mixture which forms; and the capture of electrons by the droplets. As the micron-size liquid droplets will not freeze, then vapor-mist dielectrics can be used at low temperature where many vapors have poor dielectric strength. Consequently, vapor-mist dielectrics are now being investigated* as possible cooling and insulating media for vapor-cooled pOvler trans formers.

articleTitle: A preliminary investigation into treeing, morphology and the electrical properties of polymers
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The probability of electrical breakdown in a stressed dielectric is related to the strength and time of application of the electric field. It is the aim of cable manufacturers to increase the dielectric field strength and service life without increasing the probability of failure. In this respect it is necessary to improve the quality of the insulation and prevent in-service degradation, without prohibitively increasing the cost of the product. A method which may achieve this in polymeric insulation without creating new chemical compos1t1ons is to alter the polymer morphology in such a way as to increase the “breakdown strength” and reduce the susceptibility of the material to “treeing”. Treeing appears to be the most important physical long term pre-breakdown phenomenon that occurs in dielectrics due to the externally applied electric field. Although these areas of study are obviously important, no generally accepted physical treeing model exists and there is little published work on the interrelationship between trees, electrical breakdown strength and polymer morphology. In this paper we report some interesting initial results from preliminary experimental and theoretical work relating all three subjects.

articleTitle: Future development in solid dielectric insulators for compressed gas insulated transmission systems
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Compressed gas insulated transmission lines (CGIT) have a conductor supported by solid dielectric insulators inside a metal enclosure. Sulfur hexafluoride gas at 240 kPa to 500 kPa provides the required dielectric strength. The critical dielectric design factor is usually the impulse BIL requirements. The conductor field is typically from 16 to 18 kV/mm at the BIL voltage for gas pressures of 400 to 500 kPa. This is only about 37 percent of the theoretical strength of SF<inf>6</inf> and the operating conductor fields vary from 6 percent to 14 percent depending on the system voltage.

articleTitle: Irradiation effects on charge storage in Teflon®
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: PTFE Teflon can increase both its dark conductivity and its radiation induced conductivity by factors greater than ten after receiving less than 10<sup>6</sup> rads dose. Radiation induced trapped charge leaks out or is compensated within hours in PTFE whereas other polymers maintain significant fractions of space charge for weeks. MeV electrons and <sup>60</sup>Co irradiations were used to investigate these effects in vacuum.

articleTitle: Partial discharge inception and extinction studies in polymer film structures impregnated with compressed SF6 gas
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: 1. Good consistency has been achieved in the discharge and breakdown performance of six-inch size coils wound on a new, specially-designed winding apparatus. 2. Normal probability plots indicate a single mode of breakdowns, partly determined by the conductor edge finish and partly by chance residual particles. 3. The validity of using multiple-sample test coils has been demonstrated. 4. There has been no evidence for conditioning effects on discharge behavior in tests in air or SF<inf>6</inf> gas using coils constructed with precision slit aluminum. 5. Discharge inception and extinction are affected by gas pressure in short-time tests; breakdown is not.

articleTitle: Anomalous breakdown phenomena in PMMA immersed in oil under combined direct and impulse stresses
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Anomalous breakdowns occur in synthetic solid insulating materials under combined direct and impulse stresses also.

articleTitle: Tracking and erosion consideration of physical processes
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: In 1979 it was shown that results of the inclined plane test may be affected significantly by varying the inductive impedance of the test transformer, or the ambient humidity in the test chamber. (1) It appeared that different results would also be found with tests on single samples, compared with tests with several samples in parallel.

articleTitle: Morphology of thermoplastic and cross-linked polyethylene cable insulation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The following conclusions can be drawn: 1. The study of void population, size, and mobility will help define mechanisms of electrical failure in polyethylene cable insulation. Structural models explaining the origin of voids in terms of spherulitic domains must be expanded to include nonspherulitic morphologies. 2. Sample preparation for SEM investigations is extremely important. The actions of any etching procedure used in surface preparation must be carefully characterized. 3. Oxygen plasma etching reveals differences in strain as well as differences in aged and unaged morphology near and away from the burn hole. 4. Chlorosulfonic acid treated polyethylene can be thin sectioned to study void population by TEM.

articleTitle: Modeling of thermally stimulated currents in PTFE
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The experimental evidence obtained by the combination of heat pulse and TSC techniques has provided a picture of the trap structure in PTFE. With the experimentally determined activation energies, a model has been formulated that accurately describes the TSC results. This model is based on trap controlled transport with the experimentally justified approximation that when a carrier escapes out of a trap, it immediately leaves the sample without being retrapped. Five traps were identified in the temperature range of interest with corresponding activation energies of 1.3 (2), 1.4, 1.5, and 1.7 eV. These activation energies together with the temperature maxima yield escape frequencies in the range of 10<sup>11</sup> to 10<sup>13</sup> sec<sup>−1</sup>.

articleTitle: Thermal breakdown in dielectrics
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The basic equations governing thermal breakdown are the heat flow equation equation (1) and the equation of current continuity equation (2) where the symbols have their usual meanings. The conservation of energy is expressed by Eq. 1, and it is therefore necessary. Equation 2 requires that the dielectric relaxation time ε/σ be much smaller than time intervals considered in the integration of Eq. 1. This condition holds for the examples worked below.

articleTitle: Surface properties affecting insulator flashover in vacuum
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: A longstanding difficulty in the utilization of high voltage in vacuum environments has been the relatively low electric fields withstood by insulator surfaces exposed to vacuum. The conventional remedy has been to design the insulator so that its surface is shielded from field-emitted electrons.

articleTitle: An investigation into the morphology of XLPE cable insulation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: CCl<inf>4</inf> vapour produces a quilt-like surface texture on XLPE. This results from swelling of the surface and does not correspond to the original polymer morphology.

articleTitle: A high voltage armature insulation system
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: A manufacturing process used to produce high electrical and mechanical strength homogeneous composite insulation has been described. The process features a vacuum bakeout and high pressure, hydrostatic impregnant injection. Manufacturing data and test results for a particular composite insulation system have been presented. The results are promising. Work is continuing in an effort to apply this insulation to the armature of a generator with a superconducting field winding.

articleTitle: Pre-breakdown discharges in highly non-uniform fields in relation to gas-insulated systems
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: In clean SF<inf>6</inf> gas-insulated power transmission systems significant pre-breakdown discharges are rarely observed. This is so because the prevailing electric field is only moderately non-uniform. In practical systems, however, conducting particle contamination creates regions of highly non-uniform field. Initial ionization under contaminated conditions takes the form of pre-breakdown discharges. An understanding of pre-breakdown discharges is essential for evaluating the conducting particle effects and the insulation capability of SF<inf>6</inf> gas-insulated systems.

articleTitle: Kinetics of degradation in electrically stressed polyolefins
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The need to better understand polyolefin dielectric materials has led to a long-range research project at Battelle's Columbus Laboratories sponsored by the Department of Energy, Electric Energy Systems Division.<sup>(1)</sup> As part of this project several chemical kinetic models have been hypothesized on degradation mechanistic pathways for polyolefin dielectrics under multiple stress environments. Experimental verification of these chemical kinetic mode~s by electron spin resonance (ESR) analysis techniques is underway. Some preliminary results of this research effort are discussed.

articleTitle: Corona method for investigation of charge storage and transport in dielectrics
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Corona charging methods have been widely used for the investigation of dielectric properties of solids. In conventional systems, the dielectric is charged to a given potential; only the decay of the surface potential is recorded. More complete information is obtained if charging current I<inf>0</inf> and surface voltage V(t) are recorded during as well as after corona charging. In one method the sample is charged to a constant voltage(1). In an alternative method the charging current can be controlled and kept constant(2). Such a constant current corona images the operation of an electron gun, having the advantage of giving positive as well as negative carrier deposition.

articleTitle: Thermal aging of biaxially-oriented polypropylene films part I
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Thermal aging of IPP films under some gaseous condition has been discussed from the change of physico-chemical properties. It was suggested that the thermal degradation behavior depended on the morphology and structure of the films and also on the nature of the surrounding gas. The thermal shrinkage and the increase in the crystallinity both occured sharply in the first step of thermal aging. The increase in crystallinity might be caused by reorganization or recrystallization of the isotactic-rich amorphous phase of IPP. The new melting peak around 434 K of DSC fusion curve indicates such a phase transformation. Surface degradation was made evident by the appearance of the droplets structure. The dielectric behavior of aged IPP film will be discussed in the context of these observed mophorogical change at the conference.

articleTitle: Partial discharge characteristics of liquid-impregnated laminate dielectric structures
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Evolving power conditioning system requirements in many important technological areas will place severe demands upon repetitive pulse-power components. A principal pacing system component in high reliability, repetitive pulse-power technology is the energy storage capacitor. A joint program for the research and development of repetitively operated, pulse discharge energy storage capacitors has been initiated at the Los Alamos and Sandia National Laboratories. The purpose of this ongoing activity is to create the knowledge base necessary for the design and fabrication of materials-limited, multikilojoule capacitors that are continuously operable to 100 pps with lifetimes approaching 10<sup>9</sup> charge-discharge cycles at 99.99% reliability. Recently increasing availabilities of quality plastic films, especially polypropylene, and the discovery of the excellent properties of perfluorocarbon liquids for impregnation fluids (1) make spirally-wound, plastic film/liquid impregnated capacitors the leading candidate for high energy density, repetitively operated pulse discharge energy storage devices. The dominant lifetime-limiting mechanism in this type of high energy density capacitor is a direct result of partial discharge activity at the buried foil edges, where the electric field is maximum. An initial objective of this joint program is to characterize and understand the mechanisms of this partial discharge phenomenon.

articleTitle: Electronic carrier motion in PET films
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Carrier mobility in polymers has been investigated using various experimental techniques which can be broadly classified into “fast” and “slow” techniques. The distinction is simply made by the time scale of the measurement; microseconds vs. seconds to hours. Reports have shown that these types of techniques yield vastly different mobility values. For example, Hayashi, et al. (1), using 0.1 microsecond pulsed electron beam (EB) excitation, measured electron and hole mobilities of 5 × 10<sup>−5</sup> and 5 × 10<sup>−4</sup> cm<sup>2</sup>/Vsec respectively for FEP. Gross, et al. (2), using seconds-long EB pulses, measured corresponding values of 10<sup>−16</sup> and 2 × 10<sup>−9</sup> cm<sup>2</sup>/Vsec for this material. In general, the “fast” techniques yield mobility values in the range 10<sup>−3</sup> to 10<sup>−6</sup> cm<sup>2</sup>/Vsec while the “slow” techniques yield values in the range 10<sup>−9</sup> to 10<sup>−13</sup> cm<sup>2</sup>/Vsec.

articleTitle: Fourier transform dielectric spectroscopy utilizing a real time executive (RTE) system
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The use of an RTE operating system facilitates the development of an efficient Fourier transform spectrometer which can obtain time dependent data in the four microsecond to 3000 second range. Permittivities over a frequency range of 10<sup>−4</sup> to 10<sup>4</sup> Hz are thus obtained. Program development is much easier than in more limited systems such as BCS. The Input/Output flexibility of the RTE system utilizing the HP-IB also contributes to the added capabilities. Both program development and Input/Output capabilities are used in creating time domain programming with analysis without transformation.

articleTitle: Isothermal and thermally stimulated discharge of polyethylene terephthalate foils
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: It was shown that the charging and discharging behavior of PETP can be explained in terms of an interaction between dipoles and real charges using the free volume concept. No difference between surface and bulk was found in charging and discharging experiments. In addition, the importance of the thermal history of polymer samples in charge-storage experiments is substantiated.

articleTitle: Time dependence of the radiation-induced conductivity
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Knowledge of the radiation-induced conductivity (RIC) in dielectrics is of great importance for the understanding of the charge dynamics in such materials during electron beam irradiation. In previous studies of the charge buildup, the RIC in the irradiated region was assumed to be constant in space and time (1). In 1976 Matsuoka et al. (2) improved the so-called box model introducing experimental depth-dose and charge-deposition profiles which reflect the effect of the range straggling of the incident electrons. Monte Carlo simulations (3,4) of the elastic and inelastic scattering effects during electron bombardment verified the experimental data of the space dependence of the RIC. In 1980 Gross et al. (5) showed that the time dependence of the RIC cannot be neglected, and replaced the prompt conductivity by an exponential buildup of the RIC after the onset of irradiation.

articleTitle: Electrical conductivity of anisotropic poly (paraphenylene-benzobisthiazole)
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Since the quantitative characterization of nonohmic behavior of the polymer would aid in understanding the conduction mechanism we made a series of measurements at different voltages (7). For a fiber (PPBT 28555-19-2) with an effective length of 200 µm, the axial current was quite linear up to 0.12 MV/m (the highest field available on this sample because of a design feature of the Keithley 642 electrometer which limits the maximum voltage that can be used). In future experiments still higher fields will be tried.

articleTitle: Mechanisms for inception of DC and 60 Hz AC corona in SF6
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Using a pulse-counting technique, we have measured inceptions of positive and negative point-plane corona in SF<inf>6</inf> under DC and 60 Hz AC conditions. Effects of gas pressure, UV radiation, and point electrode size on differences between AC and DC, positive and negative inceptions, were investigated. Inceptions were also calculated using the streamer criterion. Agreement was obtained with measured negative inceptions for both AC and DC conditions, but not with positive inceptions. The growth in the active electron initiation volume with applied voltage was calculated and used to explain the observed polarity effect in SF<inf>6</inf> corona inceptions. The magnitude of the polarity effect is predictably reduced either by irradiating the gap or by increasing the diameter of the point electrode. Differences between AC and DC positive inceptions are understood in terms of residual ion space charge from negative corona-enhancing avalanche-initiating electron production in the subsequent half cycle. This is consistent with the pressure dependence of negative ion mobilities in SF<inf>6</inf>. Without radiation, it is hypothesized that electron initiation for positive corona occurs mainly via field-enhanced collisional detachment of negative ions, and for negative corona via field emission from the point electrode surface.

articleTitle: Electrode material influence on the behaviour of laminated insulants subjected to inclined plane tracking tests
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The tests results reported show that the resistance-to-tracking classification of the tested materials is comparatively correct when using either S1 or S2 metal electrodes; therefore there are no reasons to prefer one of the two stainless steels.

articleTitle: Systematic study of partial discharge inception voltage in polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: We have performed measurements of partial discharges in order to observe the influence of the combination of several parameters (atmosphere, frequency and electrode radius) on the inception voltage. Similar studies such as those of Densley and Sudarshan (1), (2), Budenstein (3), Nosseir (4), Laurent et al.(5) have been performed in the past, but all of them have largely concentrated on the influence of one specific parameter. We present here a systematic experimental study where we show the effect of charge injection and the existence of relations between Paschen curve, gas electronegativity and inception voltage.

articleTitle: On the frequency dependence of water tree growth rate
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: It is demonstrated, theoretically, that the frequency dependence of the water-tree growth rate derives -at least in part- from a frequency dependent voltage drop across the tree itself. This voltage drop is associated with a dielectric relaxation of the water-droplet matrix in the host polymer. The theory explains the higher growth rate experienced at audio frequencies, and some of the variables effective in the phenomenon.

articleTitle: Light detection in polymers as a prebreakdown phenomenon
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: We explain the increase of the tree starting voltage in an outgassed specimen by the loss of a certain quantity of O<inf>2</inf>.

articleTitle: High-resolution probing of space-charge densities in Mylar electrets
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The charge density in the thickness direction of certain thin-film electrets can be determined by evaluating electrode currents caused by the irradiation of the dielectric with a partially-penetrating electron beam of adjustable energy (1). This method is capable of a resolution of about 20 percent of the respective probing depth which makes it particularly useful for the study of charge distributions in very thin dielectrics. Recently, electron-beam probing of this kind has been applied to the study of Mylar electrets (2).

articleTitle: Some effects of quartz fillers on high voltage dc resin insulation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Inorganic materials added to organic resin insulation in various concentrations offer some degree of control over certain physical and electrical properties. For example, the effect of fillers on the bulk thermal expansion and dielectric constant is well known. The use of fused silica and other inorganic fillers to help control the dc conductivity for high voltage dc insulation is presently being investigated by the author. Some preliminary results for a quartz filled bisphenol epoxy at 115°C are reported here.

articleTitle: Observations of prebreakdown and breakdown phenomena in liquid hydrocarbons II. Point-plane geometry
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Prebreakdown and breakdown phenomena have been measured optically in n-hexane, cyclohexane, isooctane and toluene using a point-plane electrode geometry. The voltage and electrode spacing were adjusted so that breakdown occurred either on the initial high voltage pulse or, in the case of a cathode point, on the positive overshoot following the initial negative pulse. The field strength for breakdown after voltage reversal is about one-third the strength determined using sphere-sphere electrodes and a unipolar pulse. The use of highly purified liquids and the point-plane electrode geometry serves to separate this study from previous ones.

articleTitle: High temperature breakdown characteristics of polyethylene film with fixed electrodes
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Impulse breakdown in high temperature range in PE is closely related with the melting of crystalline parts and its temperature dependence shows ∂F<inf>BI</inf>/∂T > 0 until a complete melting of crystalline parts. It suggests that the input energy rate from impulse electrical energy may partly be devoted to the melting of crystalline lamellae and thus enhance the breakdown voltage.

articleTitle: Surface flashover measurements in vacuill1 and N2 gas
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: An interferometric technique has been used to measure insulator surface charging in vacuum and high pressure nitrogen gas. Insulator surface charging has been observed in both cases. These data support the theory that insulator surface failure is caused by surface charging and intergap field enhancement.

articleTitle: Corona and insulation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: To the electrical insulation engineer, coronas and partial discharges are evil phenomena without other redeeming features than being warning of worse things to come. The purpose of this and the following papers is to report on your enemy, to help you better to fight and exploit him. The present paper deals with the more general fundamental aspects of coronas.

articleTitle: Transient glow discharges in laser excitation and breakdown
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The spatiotempora1 development of discharges in parallel plane gaps at high overvo1tage has been studied for many years in order to understand the physical mechanisms of breakdown. These studies have shown that a glow discharge structure is produced, even at high overvoltages where the duration of the glow discharge can be as short as tens or hundreds of nanoseconds. Recently, these transient glow discharges have been used as a pumping source for a variety of gas lasers including CO<inf>2</inf> lasers and rare gas-halide excimer lasers. Ultraviolet preionization of the gas volume is widely used to “stabilize” these laser glow discharges, i.e., to increase the energy which can be deposited into the discharge without causing a glow-to-arc transition. There has also been recent work which indicates that the corona discharges which occur in point-plane gaps have a glow discharge structure. The phenomena that are observed in these three types of discharges will be compared. We will also offer some speculations about the “corona stabilization” process that is observed in the breakdown of point-plane gaps in SF<inf>6</inf> and SF<inf>6</inf> mixtures.

articleTitle: Mechanism of protection of polyethylene by anti-treeing additives
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Water or electrochemical trees have been observed in polymeric insulation systems since the early 1970's<sup>(1,2)</sup> It is not known if water trees actually cause insulation failure(3) but they have been shown to decrease voltage breakdown strength, which is an accepted indicator of life expectancy.

articleTitle: Electroluminescence in polyethylene terephthalate (PET) (impulse voltage)
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: There have been several reports concerning the electroluminescence (EL) in polymers using ac(1,2) or impulse voltages(2,3). Several mechanisms have been considered to explain the EL in polymers. Generally, the emission will occur in two ways, that is, the emission resulted from a recombination of an electron and a hole injected from electrodes and the emission from the molecules excited, or ionized in an extreme case, by the electron with high energy, injected from electrodes or ejected from localized states and accelerated by a high electric field. Accumulation of space charges in polymers will modify the field intensity in the bulk or the surface layer of polymers and seriously affect the EL intensity.

articleTitle: Pulse corona discharges in electrostatic precipitators
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: In electrostatic precipitators (ESPs), the electric field is responsible for ion production in the vicinity of corona wires, charging of particles, and transport of charged particles to the collecting plate. In standard Cottrell type precipitators, these functions are performed by applying a DC voltage between corona electrodes and collecting plates. Because ion production requires a strongly non-uniform field, and particle transport is optimized in a uniform field, this arrangement is always a compromise and sometimes a poor one. Energizing precipitators with both a base voltage and superimposed pulse voltage, on the other hand, provides for a separation of the functions, particle transport being performed by the DC base voltage and ion production by the pulse voltage.

articleTitle: Study by far infrared spectroscopy on the changes of structure observed during the polarization of poly(vinylidene fluoride)
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Our results show that the far-infrared spectroscopy is a useful tool for characterizing the evolution of the structure of the polymer under field action: the phase transitions mechanism and the influence of the order and defects in the chains. For the α phase, poling fields up to 1 MV/cm increase the interchain order of the polymer. For the β phase these results suggest an increase of crystallinity (confirmed by X ray) but also an increase of the defects; these results must be confirmed by using poling fields stronger than 1 MV/cm. For the mixture α and β we observe a clear transition of the α to the β phase.

articleTitle: Charge transport in thin biological films grown by the Langmuir-Blodgett technique
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The present work has shown that LB films of biological molecules behave in a similar manner to the fatty acids. It has been shown that water in the films may be important in determining their properties. Further work carried out by us on the d.c. conductivity of the films has shown this to be an activated process. After vacuum pumping and application of high fields this process disappears, revealing the presence of a weakly temperature-dependent process which is due to an electron tunnelling process.

articleTitle: Theory of electrical characteristics for blocking contact MIM structures
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Electric conduction through insulating films has been the subject of intensive theoretical and experimental investigation [1–6]. However nothing definite can be said except in cases of very thin insulating films [5]. In cases of thin films [thickness > 50 A°] the d.c. electric characteristics are due to Schottky or Poole-Frenkel effects if Log I is proportional to V<sup>1/2</sup>. This can be true only if no space charge effects are present [2,3], which is generally not the case because of the poor quality of insulating films [6–8]. Furthermore, it is difficult to distinguish between the Schottky and Poole-Frenkel effects since the effective value of dielectric constant is uncertain. In fact, it is practically impossible to reach definite conclusions about the steady state characteristics due to the large number of possible charge conduction mechanisms. The non-steady state characteristics are attractive because they provide many current vs. time curves with different applied voltages for a single structure. Thus the agreement for all curves with a single set of parameters can provide a more critical test of the theory.

articleTitle: Drift-dominated unipolar conduction small-signal impedance and stability
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Many high voltage conduction models assume drift dominated conduction where each charge carrier has a constant mobility with negligible diffusion effects. Then the charge carrier velocities are proportional to the local electric field while in turn the electric field is related to the net local charge density through Gauss's law. Recent work has developed general transient time and spatial solutions of the electric field and space charge distributions and the terminal voltage - current characteristics for any initial and charge injection boundary conditions and for any type of terminal excitation or constraint (1).

articleTitle: Electrical and acoustic techniques for monitoring partial discharges
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Two different partial discharge detection systems have been described for the characterization of partial discharges in capacitor dielectric systems. One, with electrical sensors, uses computer aided control and measurement during accelerated life testing. The other, with acoustic sensors, is designed for versatility and operation in environments of high electromagnetic interference.

articleTitle: Steady-state sublinear DC conduction due to neutralization and reionization of mobile ions in polyethylene terephthalate
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Steady-state DC current vs. voltage characteristics of polyethylene terephthalate(PET) in a high temperature region are investigated. The sublinear I–V behavior is observed, and it is closely related to neutralization of mobile ions at PET-electrode metal interfaces. Steady-state DC I–V characteristic is analyzed using a model of the cyclic motion of ionic particles due to neutralization of mobile ions. The results of the analysis coincide with the experimental results. Therefore, it is concluded that the sublinear steady-state currents are due to the cyclic motion.

articleTitle: The polymorphism of carbon tetrachloride
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: A peculiarity of the polymorphic transition of CCl<inf>4</inf> was first observed by Rudman and Post (1) using X-ray and optical studies in 1966. They found that on cooling CCl<inf>4</inf> from the melt, a face-centred cubic phase is formed. However, this face-centred cubic phase or phase I is transformed spontaneously to a rhombohedral or phase II if left at this temperature for a few hours. This rhombohedral phase is then followed by a transformation to a monoclinic phase or the glassy phase III. On warming of the glassy phase, the rhombohedral phase is formed and this phase persists until it melts.

articleTitle: Diffusion studies of antioxidants in polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The successful use of polymeric insulating materials in electrotechnical applications requires a long-term stabilization of their initially excellent mechanical and electrical properties against degradation. One of the usual means of stabilization is to add special additives at low concentration levels. Apart from the necessary chemical effectiveness, the additives have to comply with certain physical requirements: The additive should be homogeneously distributed within the polymer, it should be sufficiently soluble and it should also be retained over extended periods of time. The questions pertaining to these problems can be answered by studying the local additive concentration and its time-dependence in respective systems.

articleTitle: On the unifying admittance calculation, part II
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Strictly speaking, neither the ideal resistance bridge arm nor capacitance or inductance bridge arm exist in an AC bridge arm. The phase angle difference in all arms (φ<inf>1</inf>, φ<inf>2</inf>, φ<inf>3</inf>, and φ<inf>4</inf>) are algebraic quantities with definite magnitude and positive or negative sign and this is true with the corresponding loss angles (1, 2). In a capacitance loss bridge, the fundamental property of an algebraic quantity being positive or negative value is violated by the equation δ=90−|φ| of the sample arms, so the separate equilibrium calculation of the value-phase is hampered and it will be even more difficult to make use of the equilibrium equation (φ<inf>1</inf> + φ<inf>4</inf> = φ<inf>2</inf> + φ<inf>3</inf>) of the phase angle. In order to use this equation, the unifying admittance calculation must be adopted. The two kinds of unifying calculation are equivalent and either can be used. The results of the two kinds of phase equilibrium of the Schering loss bridge are compared with those obtained by other scientists in the past 50 years in Table 1. It can be seen that very few researchers have strictly abided by the unifying impedance calculation and their studies have been confined to the simplest bridges. Most investigators have not placed emphasis on the unifying calculation. Nevertheless, their results coincided with those obtained by the unifying admittance calculation. Therefore, it is clear that the unifying admittance calculation method has reflected the objective need of people.

articleTitle: Design and development of a fast rise time high voltage pulse transformer using solid dielectric materials
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: A high voltage pulse transformer has been developed for use in firing individual stage spark gaps in multi-megavolt Marx generators. The design incorporates the use of capacitor winding techniques with epoxy impregnating medium. The result is a reliable device with high mechanical and electrical strength.

articleTitle: Theoretical properties of streamers in solid dielectrics
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: A model has previously been described (1,2) which provides for the self-consistent numerical description of the spatially and temporally coherent evolution of electron avalanches in solid dielectrics. Various features of the propagating negative tip of the avalanche have been presented (1), and speculations were offered about the possible importance of recurring processes at the positive tip leading to cathode directed streamer formation and subsequent breakdown (2). An extensive set of numerical calculations has now been performed within this model framework. The purpose of the calculations was to explore the dependence of important calculational features on the input parameters of the model. A preliminary description of the results of this parameter study is given in this note. The research is part of an ongoing program to understand the charging and discharging properties of electron beam irradiated solid dielectrics.

articleTitle: Impulse dielectric breakdown of multi stress aged polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The tests have shown that the 1.2/50µs impulse dielectric strength of unaged polyethylene is of the range of 150 kV/mm. The impulse breakdown stress of that polyethylene can decrease during its life time to 60–50% of the original value. The rate of decrease depends on the conditions of aging. At particular electric stress and temperature, the fastest rate occurs when polyethylene is aged in presence of water and/or partial discharges. The impulse voltage strength remains significantly higher and the influence of aging voltage and temperature less detectable when these two factors are limited.

articleTitle: Electric breakdown of plasma polymerized styrene thin films
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Electric breakdown of PPS was studied by taking advantage of self-healing. On the basis of the results a new simple breakdown model was presented in which tunnelling emission from the cathode controls the conduction current and the impulse thermal process governs the breakdown in PPS. The numerically calculated values obtained by discarding the space charge can be fitted to the F<inf>B</inf>-T<inf>O</inf>, and F<inf>B</inf>-α curves when Φ<inf>D</inf> is about 1 eV, and are also consistent with all the experimental results. It was also found from the experimental results that space charge can be neglected provided μ<inf>p</inf> is beyond a certain value even though the steady state avalanche is taken into accuont.

articleTitle: Interaction of corona with dielectric materials leading to damage
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: From experimental results obtained with polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene terephthalate, the authors consider the transformation phase of an insulator when it is submitted to discharges during short periods (1 < t < 1800 s). The effect of high pressure discharges was investigated by gas chromatography using the polymer as the stationary phase. By varying the atmosphere where discharges are produced and varying the time of treatment, a critical time t<inf>c</inf> has been defined. This time corresponds to the minimum for a specific retention volume of a solute. The same time is observed when infrared analysis is made, for example, on PP and compared to a loss tangent measurement. A rapid increase in the loss of polymer corresponds to an increase of CO and CC absorptions for the same t<inf>c</inf>. This time seems to correspond to a limit between the transformation and the degradation of polymer under 60 Hz voltages. Degradation is considered for cross-linked polyethylene (XLPE) and the effect of moisture is emphasized in terms of electrical measurements.

articleTitle: Laboratory testing of electrical insulating materials superficial resistance to HF vapours as selection criteria for SF6 circuit breakers insulators
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Electrical insulating materials show a temporal drop of electric surface resistivity R<inf>S</inf> when exposed to SF<inf>6</inf> electric arc decomposition products atmosphere. A general curve run had been presented /fig.1/ and three important points R<inf>o</inf>,R<inf>min</inf> and R<inf>e</inf> were marked on the curve [1].

articleTitle: Calculation of insulation void density and size from partial discharge pulse height analysis
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Although the results presented give good agreement to the known void volumes, some areas of the theoretical approach need to be refined in the light of experimental data. The most important is equation (3). This equation predicts the number of PDs is a linearly increasing function of the applied voltage. However, frequently the numbers of PDs will decrease with increasing voltages.

articleTitle: The nature of pyroelectricity in polyvinylidene fluoride at low temperatures
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The dynamic pyroelectric response in PVF<inf>2</inf> in the low temperature range of −55°C to −10°C, which includes the α<inf>a</inf>-relaxation of the polymer, is of dipolar origin and it arises from reorientation of the non-permanent dipoles in the amorphous phase.

articleTitle: The feasibility of identifying and locating thermal mechanisms in large machines by remote sensing
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: In order to obtain an early warning of any over-heating problem within large electrical machines, instruments have been designed and are now commercially available, called ‘Condition Monitors’ (C.M.). Their function is to produce an electrical signal when any particles/materials, i.e. as emitted by over heated insulation, pass through the sensitive ion chamber. In the USA, considerable success has been claimed in preventing catastrophic failure of machines by responding to the condition monitor signals and removing the machine from load. However, electricity suppliers are generally cautious in responding to any condition monitor signal, resulting in either load shedding or desynchronisation of the machine. At present a condition monitor signal will not indicate to the operator the cause for the alarm, nor its location within the machine, even if it is an over heating problem. If the cause for the alarm can be identified and it is a thermal process which can be related to a particular material, then the relative importance of the alarm can probably be assessed. However, these processes are time consuming and often interpretation of the results is difficult and inconclusive. Certain techniques will be discussed, together with promising new developments.

articleTitle: Molecular basis of pyroelectricity in PVDF
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The piezofilm possessed a slight curl, indicating how it had once been wound on a roll: the convex side was previously the outer side. Invariably the outer side was found to be polarized positively, as determined by the sign of the thermally stimulated currents.

articleTitle: Electrical conductivity and thermal decomposition of high temperature phenolic- and silicone-based materials
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: The temperature dependence of the electrical conductivity and thermal decomposition characteristics of several phenolic and silicone resins reinforced with glass chopped fabric or cloth have been measured to 600–700°C in a nitrogen atmosphere. Thermal data were obtained using mass spectroscopy and thermal gravimetric analysis. Peaks in the conductivity temperature dependence and deviations from ohmic behavior are found to be associated with material decomposition and/or outgassing. Results show a direct correlation between thermal stability and temperature dependent electrical characteristics.

articleTitle: Short circuit TSO currents
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Short circuit thermally stimulated discharge [TSO) has been used as a technique to study trapping characteristics of a material(1). We have in mind experiments in which the sample is initially poled under constant applied voltage V<inf>0</inf> through an ohmic contact, until a steady state current i<inf>S</inf> is reached. It was shown by Many and Rakavy that, for a single trap level and trapping time greater than the transit time, the transient current is the sum of i<inf>S</inf> and a negative exponential, dependent on the trapping and de-trapping parameters(2). This simple result comes out because an electrostatic equilibrium is reached, which, afterwards is not changed during the trapping process. It may be concluded that if the temperature were now changed, keeping V<inf>0</inf> on, the change in the current would reflect the change in the free charge population, due to the decrease or increase [temperature up or down) of the de-trapping time. We are assuming that the free mobility μ is independent on the temperature, but it may be shown that the electrostatic equilibrium would not be destroyed even if μ were temperature dependent.

articleTitle: Electrochemical deterioration of semi-conducting glaze on insulator surfaces
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: A successful accelerated corrosion test method, the wick test, has been developed to simulate the corrosion process of semi-conductively glazed material in actual operation. The wick test is efficient and reproduces the characteristics of semi-conducting glaze corrosion that can be expected to occur under operating conditions. Through wick test, some of the parameters affecting the deterioration rate were studied.

articleTitle: Some speculations concerning certain minor mysteries
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1981
abstract: Sometimes we come across some small features of a physical problem which seem a little puzzling or odd. Such points are occasionally the key which gives us a new insight into some basic truth. This paper is concerned with three problems, two of which have some paradoxical features, while the third is about an interesting new hypothesis which has not yet been fully analysed.
